content: The Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) is the causative agent of Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (AIDS) and represents one of the most significant infectious disease burdens worldwide. It is the fifth leading cause of disability across all age groups. HIV belongs to the Retroviridae family and primarily targets immune system cells, including CD4+ T cells, dendritic cells, and macrophages. There are two serotypes of HIV, with HIV-1 being the most virulent and pathogenic. HIV is transmitted through various routes, including sexual fluids (vaginal and semen), blood via percutaneous inoculation, vertical transmission from mother to fetus through the placenta, and breast milk. With the advent of antiretroviral therapy (ART), HIV is now considered a chronic illness, most commonly observed in men who have sex with men. Early symptoms of HIV infection are nonspecific, but as the disease progresses to its final stage, AIDS, patients develop opportunistic infections due to severe immunosuppression. Diagnosis of HIV is achieved through methods such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR), enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), Western blot, and rapid antigen testing. ART and vaccines have shown promising results in the treatment and prevention of HIV, respectively. Prevention remains a cornerstone of HIV management, and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends routine screening for high-risk groups, including men who have sex with men, pregnant women, drug users, and sexually active heterosexuals. Despite advancements in treatment, HIV remains a serious disease requiring ongoing efforts in surveillance and education by healthcare providers. The World Health Organization (WHO) and CDC classify HIV-infected individuals based on their CD4+ T cell count: Stage A: Asymptomatic, with a CD4+ count >500/μL. Stage B: Mild symptoms or AIDS-related complex symptoms, with a CD4+ count between 400/μL and 200/μL. Stage C: AIDS-defining illnesses, with a CD4+ count <200/μL. As the CD4+ count drops below 200/μL, patients are at increased risk of developing opportunistic infections and neoplasms. For patients suspected of having HIV in regions with high prevalence, diagnostic approaches include rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs), enzyme immunoassays (EIAs), chemiluminescence immunoassays (CLIAs), and electrochemiluminescence immunoassays (ELAs). The most effective treatment regimen for HIV is highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART), which typically includes a combination of two nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) and one drug from a different class. Commonly used drugs include tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF), tenofovir alafenamide (TAF), and others targeting specific pathways such as CCR5. Recommendations for HIV Management: Do's: Perform HLA-B5701 testing before initiating abacavir to avoid hypersensitivity reactions. Monitor complete blood count (CBC) with differentials when prescribing zidovudine. Assess glomerular filtration rate (GFR) when starting TAF or TDF. Don'ts: Avoid prescribing tenofovir in patients with renal impairment or bone disease. Do not use nevirapine in patients with hepatic impairment.
